useCases.title: Cryptographically Verifiable Digital Product Passports for EU Battery Regulation Compliance
useCases.summary: AAS Studio helps manufacturers comply with the EU Battery Regulation (2023/1542) and wider Digital Product Passport requirements by turning existing PDF datasheets into a signed, verifiable product passport. The problem: OEMs and battery makers already hold the required data, but not in the IDTA Asset Administration Shell format regulators expect, and building that tooling from scratch is a multi-month integration project. AAS Studio extracts and maps the data with AI, lets an engineer review it, and issues a W3C Verifiable Credential (VCDM 2.0, JWT-VC and SD-JWT-VC) with a cryptographic hash anchored to the passport content. The organization (manufacturer) is the issuer. The credential has no personal holder: the product itself is what the passport describes, resolved via a GS1 Digital Link URL rather than carried in a personal wallet. Verifiers are regulators, recyclers, and downstream supply-chain partners, who check the signature offline against a public JWKS with no account and no callback to AAS Studio. Revocation runs on a Bitstring/Token Status List.
useCases.userJourney: A manufacturer uploads an existing product datasheet (PDF) into AAS Studio. The AI extracts the relevant fields and maps them onto the IDTA Asset Administration Shell submodel required for the target regulation (Battery Passport, EU Machinery, or Catena-X SerialPart). An engineer at the organization reviews the mapped data and approves it, since the tool never signs anything unreviewed. On approval, AAS Studio computes a canonical content hash and issues a W3C Verifiable Credential (ES256-signed JWT-VC and SD-JWT-VC), and allocates a revocation slot on a Bitstring/Token Status List. The signed record and a QR code resolving via GS1 Digital Link are handed to the manufacturer to attach to the product or packaging. Any downstream party who needs to check the passport (a regulator, a recycler, a supply-chain partner) scans or opens the link and verifies the signature entirely offline against a public JWKS, with no account and no server round-trip required. There is no personal wallet step: the organization issues directly to a public verifier via API, matching the "business wallet" pattern Harmen described.

useCases.title: Cryptographically Verifiable Digital Product Passports for EU Battery Regulation Compliance
useCases.summary:
European manufacturers must issue Digital Product Passports (EU Battery Regulation
2023/1542, from 18 February 2027, with the ESPR extending this to further
categories). Today the data those passports need lives in unstructured PDF
datasheets, and manufacturers have no way to prove a downstream party has not
altered the file after publication.

AAS Studio turns a datasheet into a conformant Asset Administration Shell (IDTA,
IEC 63278-1:2023), then issues a W3C Verifiable Credential (VCDM 2.0, JWT-VC, and
an SD-JWT-VC variant with selective disclosure) committing to a canonical hash of
the passport content. The manufacturer is the issuer, signing with a tenant-scoped
ES256 key. Any verifier — regulator, recycler, supply-chain partner — checks the
credential against a public JWKS with no account and no call back to AAS Studio:
verification is fully offline. Revocation is enforced via a Bitstring/Token Status
List.
useCases.userJourney:
1. Manufacturer uploads a PDF datasheet; AAS Studio extracts the regulatory fields
   with an LLM ensemble and maps them onto a conformant Asset Administration Shell,
   validated against the official IDTA test engine.
2. AAS Studio computes a canonical hash of the passport content and issues a W3C
   Verifiable Credential signed with the manufacturer's own ES256 key, optionally
   as an SD-JWT-VC for selective disclosure.
3. If issued as revocable, a Bitstring/Token Status List slot is allocated; the
   manufacturer can revoke it later, effective immediately for any verifier.
4. The holder presents the credential's JWT to a relying party by any channel.
5. The relying party verifies it fully offline: it fetches the public JWKS and
   re-derives the proof itself, including the status-list check, so the verdict
   never depends on trusting AAS Studio's server.
